Chapter 4: Faith in Action — The Meaning and Limits of Forgiveness
When news of the Nickel Mines shooting reached far beyond the Amish community, it left people everywhere asking the same questions.
How could forgiveness come so quickly—and so completely? Some people looked at the Amish response with admiration, seeing it as a beautiful example of faith put into practice. Others weren’t so sure. Was that kind of forgiveness even real? Was it healthy to forgive so soon? And does forgiveness mean you’re just forgetting, or excusing, what happened?
For the Amish, these aren’t new questions. Their understanding of forgiveness has grown out of centuries of teachings and lived experience.
You see, forgiveness isn’t about wiping the slate clean or pretending the pain never existed.
It’s about letting go of resentment and trusting that justice—real justice—belongs to God. That doesn’t mean wrongdoers avoid consequences, or that victims are supposed to act like nothing happened.
Instead, forgiveness becomes a way to heal. It’s a gift not just to the one who’s forgiven, but also to the one who forgives.
After the shooting, some Amish families found themselves caught between the need for forgiveness and the deep longing for justice. Grief was real. The loss of their children was overwhelming, and anger and confusion crept in.
Still, even in their heartbreak, they chose to offer grace. Not because they didn’t feel anger, but because their faith taught them it was the right thing to do.
For them, forgiveness wasn’t an emotion—it was a decision rooted in faith.
This idea became even more important as outsiders—reporters, visitors—started asking questions. How could the Amish forgive so quickly? Were they pushing down their feelings, or just denying what happened?
With patience, the Amish explained: forgiveness doesn’t mean forgetting or excusing harm. It means refusing to let anger and bitterness take over your life.
There’s one story that really stands out. A father, heartbroken over his daughter, described forgiveness as a way to keep his heart open. He didn’t pretend the pain was gone, or that justice didn’t matter. But he simply wouldn’t allow hate to define his life.
Forgiveness, for him, was a way to honor his daughter’s memory—and to trust that, somehow, God would bring healing in time.
The Amish also know there are limits to forgiveness. They don’t expect wounds to heal overnight, or memories to simply fade away. Some hurts take years to mend. But they believe forgiveness is the first step toward wholeness.
By letting go of anger, they make room for hope and renewal.
Most people don’t realize how much courage forgiveness takes—especially when the pain is still fresh. For the Amish, that courage comes from a deep trust in God and a belief that grace is always possible.
They don’t pretend to have all the answers, and they certainly aren’t free from struggle. But they choose, again and again, to walk the path of forgiveness—believing it’s the only way to find peace in a world that’s often broken.
